title: Probability of Dependent Events and Combined Probability
topic: Probability - Dependent Events and Without Replacement
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that the first ball is red?
questions.explanation: Total balls = 8. Red balls = 5. P(first red) = 5/8.

questions.question: Using the same bag (5 red, 3 blue), if the first ball drawn is red, what is the probability that the second ball is also red?
questions.explanation: After drawing one red ball, there are 7 balls left (4 red, 3 blue). P(second red after first red) = 4/7.

questions.question: Using the same bag (5 red, 3 blue), what is the probability of drawing two red balls without replacement?
questions.explanation: P(both red) = P(first red) x P(second red after first red) = 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

questions.question: Two events are dependent if the occurrence of one event _______ the probability of the other event.
questions.explanation: Dependent events are events where the outcome of one event affects (changes) the probability of the other event occurring.

questions.question: A box contains 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of drawing a green then a yellow?
questions.explanation: P(green first) = 4/10. After drawing green, 9 marbles remain (6 yellow). P(yellow second) = 6/9. P(green then yellow) = 4/10 x 6/9 = 24/90 = 4/15.

questions.question: Using the same box (4 green, 6 yellow), what is the probability of drawing a yellow then a green without replacement?
questions.explanation: P(yellow first) = 6/10. After drawing yellow, 9 marbles remain (4 green). P(green second) = 4/9. P(yellow then green) = 6/10 x 4/9 = 24/90 = 4/15.

questions.question: From the previous two questions, what is the probability of drawing one green and one yellow in any order without replacement?
questions.explanation: P(one of each) = P(green then yellow) + P(yellow then green) = 4/15 + 4/15 = 8/15.

questions.question: A deck of 52 cards has 4 aces. Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are aces?
questions.explanation: P(first ace) = 4/52. After drawing one ace, 51 cards remain (3 aces). P(second ace) = 3/51. P(both aces) = 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.

questions.question: For dependent events A and B, which formula is correct?
options: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B after A occurs)
questions.explanation: For dependent events: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B after A occurs). The probability of B changes depending on whether A has occurred.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 red, 4 blue, and 5 green balls. One ball is drawn without replacement. What is the total number of balls?
questions.explanation: Total = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 balls.

questions.question: Using the bag from the previous question (3 red, 4 blue, 5 green), two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of drawing two blue balls?
questions.explanation: P(first blue) = 4/12 = 1/3. After drawing one blue, 11 balls remain (3 blue). P(second blue) = 3/11. P(both blue) = 1/3 x 3/11 = 3/33 = 1/11.

questions.question: A class has 12 boys and 8 girls. Two students are selected randomly without replacement. What is the probability that both are girls?
questions.explanation: Total = 20. P(first girl) = 8/20 = 2/5. After selecting one girl, 19 students remain (7 girls). P(second girl) = 7/19. P(both girls) = 2/5 x 7/19 = 14/95.

questions.question: Using the same class (12 boys, 8 girls), what is the probability that both students selected are boys?
questions.explanation: P(first boy) = 12/20 = 3/5. After selecting one boy, 19 students remain (11 boys). P(second boy) = 11/19. P(both boys) = 3/5 x 11/19 = 33/95.

questions.question: Using the same class (12 boys, 8 girls), what is the probability of selecting one boy and one girl in any order?
Three cards are drawn from a deck of 52 without replacement. What is the probability that all three are hearts?
questions.explanation: P(first heart) = 13/52. After one heart drawn, P(second heart) = 12/51. After two hearts drawn, P(third heart) = 11/50. P(all hearts) = 13/52 x 12/51 x 11/50 = 1716/132600 = 11/850.

questions.question: A jar contains 6 black and 4 white balls. Three balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that all three are black?
questions.explanation: P(first black) = 6/10. P(second black) = 5/9. P(third black) = 4/8. P(all black) = 6/10 x 5/9 x 4/8 = 120/720 = 1/6.

questions.question: When drawing without replacement, the probability of the second event depends on the _______ of the first event.
questions.explanation: In dependent events without replacement, the outcome of the first event determines what remains and affects the probability of the second event.

questions.question: A bag contains 7 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both balls are the same colour?
Using the same bag (7 red, 3 blue), what is the probability that the two balls drawn are different colours?
questions.explanation: P(different colours) = 1 - P(same colour) = 1 - 24/45 = 21/45 = 7/15.

questions.question: A committee of 2 is to be formed from 5 men and 4 women. What is the probability that both members are women?
questions.explanation: Total = 9. P(first woman) = 4/9. After selecting one woman, 8 people remain (3 women). P(second woman) = 3/8. P(both women) = 4/9 x 3/8 = 12/72 = 1/6.

questions.question: From a group of 3 doctors and 5 nurses, two people are selected randomly. What is the probability that at least one is a doctor?
questions.explanation: P(no doctors) = P(both nurses) = 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. P(at least one doctor) = 1 - 5/14 = 9/14.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. What is the probability of drawing a king followed by a queen?
questions.explanation: P(king first) = 4/52. After drawing a king, 51 cards remain (4 queens). P(queen second) = 4/51. P(king then queen) = 4/52 x 4/51 = 16/2652 = 4/663.

questions.question: What is the probability of drawing a king followed by another king from a standard deck without replacement?
questions.explanation: P(king first) = 4/52. After drawing a king, 51 cards remain (3 kings). P(second king) = 3/51. P(two kings) = 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.

questions.question: A bag contains 10 balls numbered 1 to 10. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both numbers are even?
questions.explanation: Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (5 balls). P(first even) = 5/10 = 1/2. After drawing one even, 9 balls remain (4 even). P(second even) = 4/9. P(both even) = 1/2 x 4/9 = 4/18 = 2/9.

questions.question: Using the same bag (balls 1-10), what is the probability that both numbers drawn are odd?
questions.explanation: Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (5 balls). P(first odd) = 5/10 = 1/2. After drawing one odd, 9 balls remain (4 odd). P(second odd) = 4/9. P(both odd) = 1/2 x 4/9 = 4/18 = 2/9.

questions.question: Using the same bag (balls 1-10), what is the probability that one number is odd and one is even?
questions.explanation: P(one odd, one even) = 1 - P(both odd) - P(both even) = 1 - 2/9 - 2/9 = 1 - 4/9 = 5/9.

questions.question: A shelf has 8 fiction and 5 non-fiction books. Two books are selected randomly without replacement. What is the probability that the first is fiction and the second is non-fiction?
questions.explanation: Total = 13. P(fiction first) = 8/13. After selecting fiction, 12 books remain (5 non-fiction). P(non-fiction second) = 5/12. P = 8/13 x 5/12 = 40/156 = 10/39.

questions.question: In the previous question, what is the probability of selecting both fiction books?
questions.explanation: P(first fiction) = 8/13. After selecting one fiction, 12 books remain (7 fiction). P(second fiction) = 7/12. P(both fiction) = 8/13 x 7/12 = 56/156 = 14/39.

questions.question: A box contains 4 defective and 8 good items. Two items are selected without replacement. What is the probability that both are good?
questions.explanation: Total = 12. P(first good) = 8/12 = 2/3. After selecting one good, 11 items remain (7 good). P(second good) = 7/11. P(both good) = 2/3 x 7/11 = 14/33.

questions.question: Using the previous box (4 defective, 8 good), what is the probability that at least one item is defective?
questions.explanation: P(at least one defective) = 1 - P(both good) = 1 - 14/33 = 19/33.

questions.question: A jar has 5 red, 4 blue, and 3 green sweets. Two sweets are taken without replacement. What is the probability of getting a red followed by a green?
questions.explanation: Total = 12. P(red first) = 5/12. After drawing red, 11 sweets remain (3 green). P(green second) = 3/11. P = 5/12 x 3/11 = 15/132 = 5/44.

questions.question: Using the same jar (5 red, 4 blue, 3 green), what is the probability of getting two different colours?
Compare: Drawing with replacement makes events _______, while drawing without replacement makes events _______.
questions.explanation: With replacement: items are returned, probabilities stay the same (independent). Without replacement: items are removed, probabilities change (dependent).

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.6 and P(B after A occurs) = 0.5, what is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: For dependent events: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B after A occurs) = 0.6 x 0.5 = 0.30.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A and B) = 0.2, are A and B independent?
options: Yes, because P(A) x P(B) = P(A and B)
No, because P(A) + P(B) is not equal to P(A and B)
Yes, because P(A) + P(B) > P(A and B)
No, because P(A) x P(B) is not equal to P(A and B)
questions.explanation: Events are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Here, 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2, which equals P(A and B). So yes, they are independent.
